boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Golymin entry (engagement, 26 December 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Marshal Augereau's 7th corps, the 1st and, from nightfall, 2nd divisions of Marshal Davout's 3rd corps and the Grand Duke of Berg's reserve cavalry against Prince Gallizin's Russian detachment, with troops of General Dochtorow's 7th Division and, from 3 in the afternoon, Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz, at Golymin, from Gallizin's arrival at 8 in the morning to the Russian retreat on Makow in the night. Side B's retreat to Golymin on 25 and 26 December, the orders of 26 December and the movements of the other French corps are context. The battle of Pultusk on the same day, a separate entry, the fighting at Czarnowo, Nasielsk and Sonsk before it, and the pursuit from the morning of 27 December are outside this entry; the guns and vehicles the Russians abandoned on the French march and those taken on the road to Gotskowo are reported with their place and time. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 27,000 men under Marshal Davoust and side B (Russian) 22,000 men under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin at Golymin on 26 December 1806, with no battalions, squadrons or guns. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. No passage read gives either side's engaged strength. The summary return Foucart prints makes 47,200 for the 7th corps, the 1st reserve cavalry corps and the 3rd corps together (our arithmetic), but these are whole corps in the middle of December, not the troops engaged (claim side-a-strength). For side B Höpfner gives no total (claim hoepfner-side-b); the Grand Duke of Berg wrote that they had all generally thought the enemy had 50,000 men, more than twice Bodart's 22,000 (claim foucart-side-b; our comparison); the 20,000 men that, by the peasants' account in the report on General Durosnel's brigade, had passed Pomorze since the night, part of them toward Pultusk, are not a count of the force at Golymin (claim foucart-side-b; our reading). Which source Bodart used was not checked. The forces at hand followed the commanders' decisions (claims side-a-decisions and side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 26/12. Engagement at Golymin (6.)'; 'victory of the French (27,000 men) under Marshal Davoust over the Russians (22,000 men) under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin'. 'Gen.-Lt.' is General-Leutnant and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side B (Russian) in Höpfner, who gives no total. Prince Gallizin's column reached Golymin at 8 in the morning of the 26th after a march of 13 hours. On the 25th the prince had kept with him the detachment cut off from General Sacken, the Dnieper Musketeer and Little-Russian Cuirassier Regiments, and had sent 1 battalion and 2 squadrons to take in 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars pushed away from General Count Pahlen, who had stayed behind at Lopaczyn with a rear guard of the 21st Jäger Regiment, the Sumy Hussar Regiment and a horse battery, and held the crossing there until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was blocked and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off. General Dochtorow, commander of the 7th Division, had his division march off and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin; by Gallizin's report Dochtorow seems to have stayed with the whole division. Colonel Kreuz had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars. Gallizin sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment, detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns, pushed forward 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons, and posted the rest before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; in reserve the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars and the troops of the 7th Division. He reinforced the Kostroma regiment with 1 battalion of the Taurian Grenadier Regiment, and later sent forward the 2nd battalion of that regiment and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiment, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons not yet in action. At 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz joined him from Ciechanowo, and took a lively part in the combat on the right wing, though in what way, Höpfner writes, is nowhere stated; Tschaplitz had the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, the history of side B's ally, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102 and 122-126). He gives no total for side B or for any regiment, says that Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's account and the French reports in Mathieu Dumas differ so completely that his account is only an attempt, and follows Danielewski for Dochtorow's force (dependency note). The 2 squadrons of hussars cut off from Pahlen are, we take it, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars pushed away from him that Gallizin took in on the 25th, and these the 2 squadrons with Colonel Kreuz and in the reserve at Golymin (our reading). Höpfner spells the prince Gallizin, Bodart Gallitzin. The force at hand followed the field marshal's orders and the generals' decisions (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'Prince Gallizin sent ahead to Golymin to inform General Dochtorow of his approach, and to ask him to take him in with the 7th Division, as he [was] from two sides by the enemy' (p. 101); 'threatened' (p. 102); 'at 8 in the morning of the 26th the column, after a march of 13 hours, reached Golymin, 1½ Meilen away'; 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'at that time the detachment cut off from General Sacken, which had stood below Lopaczyn, namely the Dnieper Musketeer and Little-Russian Cuirassier Regiments, arrived at Slubowo on its march to Strzegocin'; 'the prince kept it with him, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession'; 'at the same time another enemy cavalry detachment arrived from the direction of Lopaczyn, pursuing 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars that had been pushed away from General Count Pahlen'; 'Prince Gallizin sent forward 1 battalion and 2 squadrons to take in the hussars, so that on this side too the enemy confined himself to a skirmish of flankers, which lasted until 3 in the afternoon'; 'General Count Pahlen had stayed behind at Lopaczyn with a rear guard — the 21st Jäger Regiment, the Sumy Hussar Regiment and a horse battery'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; '1) We follow here General Danielewski's statement, whereas according to Prince Gallizin's report General Dochtorow seems to have stayed behind with the whole division'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); 'while, to cover the left wing, thus probably in the direction of Strzegocin, 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons were pushed forward' (p. 124); 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'when the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment came under the fire of the enemy's skirmishers, it at once gave way, but Prince Tscherbatow led it forward again with the colour in his hand, and Prince Gallizin reinforced the regiment further with 1 battalion of the Taurian Grenadier Regiment'; 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'after their arrival they had taken a lively part in the combat on the right wing, but in what way is nowhere stated'; 'at Ciechanowo he united with General Tschaplitz, who, as mentioned, had had to advance from Golymin to Ciechanowo with the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division'; 'the Russian report of Prince Gallizin in Plotho's Tagebuch, the report in General Danielewski's work and the French reports in Mathieu Dumas etc. on this combat differ so completely from one another that the account given here may be regarded only as an attempt to make the course of the combat to some extent clear'.

claims.value: Side B (Russian) in the French documents Foucart prints. Marshal Davout reported on 26 December that a column of artillery, cavalry and infantry that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice the day before. The 3rd corps's journal has a considerable line of Russian cavalry in front of the woods and on the road to Golymin, and the 1st division fighting an infantry ten times stronger and 12 to 15 pieces of cannon. General Rapp wrote that the enemy infantry was supported by about 1,500 cavalry. The Grand Duke of Berg reported the enemy resting his left on a wood held by some battalions of infantry and his right on a small village by a great line of cavalry supported by several lines of infantry, and, when he later had Golymin reconnoitred, a small wood held with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon; they had all generally thought the enemy had 50,000 men, all the troops that had evacuated Plonsk, Nasielsk, Nowemiasto and Ciechanow having united on Golymin. General Curély recalled about 1,000 horses of the cuirassiers of the Russian Guard and dragoons, 8 or 10 pieces in battery, the Russian army, coming from Pultusk, filing along the road through Golymin to Makow, and, where the brigade Lasalle was to charge the Russian artillery, not a horseman or a foot soldier but 7 or 8 cannon. A report on General Durosnel's light cavalry brigade, signed by him at Pomorze at 2 in the afternoon, has a strong Russian column of cavalry and infantry filing past Pomorze from about 10 o'clock for a couple of hours, the enemy putting much cavalry in line without returning a carbine shot, and, by the peasants' account, 20,000 men passing there since the night, part heading for Pultusk and part taking a road to the left. General Corbineau wrote at 10 in the evening that the enemy was in very great numbers at Kalenczyn; that there was cannon with this force, which had fired three shots, though whether it had several pieces could not be judged; that the night prevented judging the enemy's strength, but that it was considerable, to judge by the movement seen for two hours by the light of the burning village of Kalenczyn; and that two wounded dragoons who had crossed the enemy force called it very numerous, as did General Amey. The editor writes that the Russians filing toward Golymin at the beginning of the engagement, presenting their left flank, were the column the dragoons' reconnaissance had seen on the 25th, coming not from Pultusk but from Bielice; and that another column, repulsed at Sonsk on the 25th by the Grand Duke and marching from Ciechanow on Pultusk, which General Durosnel saw file past Pomorze from 10 o'clock to noon heading for Golymin, the division Panin, came out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon on the left flank of the 7th corps.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 473, 474, 476, 478-480, 482, 484, 485, 487 and 490-492). None of these is a return: Davout's 'very numerous', the Grand Duke's general opinion of 50,000, the peasants' 20,000 and Corbineau's 'considerable' are impressions or hearsay, the journal's 'ten times stronger' is a comparison, and Rapp's about 1,500 cavalry, the Grand Duke's 4,000 infantry in the wood and Curély's about 1,000 horses are observers' estimates of parts of the force. The 50,000 is more than twice Bodart's 22,000 (claim bodart-strength; our comparison). The peasants' 20,000 passed Pomorze, part of them toward Pultusk, and are not a count of the force at Golymin (our reading). The report on Durosnel's brigade is printed without a heading and closes with his signature. The editor's column 'not from Pultusk but from Bielice' contradicts Curély's Russian army coming from Pultusk (our comparison). His column repulsed at Sonsk and coming out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon corresponds to Höpfner's General Pahlen, who took up a position at Sonsk on the 25th, and General Tschaplitz, who ran into Durosnel's brigade at Pomorze with him and joined Gallizin at 3 (claims side-b-command and hoepfner-side-b; our comparison); Höpfner names no division Panin in the passages read, and has Durosnel's and Wathier's light cavalry brigades, not the Grand Duke, attack Pahlen at Sonsk. The phase is unresolved, as in claim hoepfner-side-b. English renderings (ours): Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'yesterday¹, as I had the honour to report to you, a column of artillery, cavalry and infantry that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'the Russians had a considerable line of cavalry in front of the woods and on the road to Golymin'; 'the dragoons were placed in reserve behind the 1st division'; 'this division had fought without artillery (it had not been able to follow because of the bad roads) against an infantry ten times stronger and 12 to 15 pieces of cannon....'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'the enemy infantry had many advantages over us, being able to withdraw at the quick step; it was supported by about 1,500 cavalry, who made a show of waiting for us while the infantry filed off'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'my advance guard made its junction with Marshal Davout's corps at the village of Garnowo at the same time as I was reconnoitring by my left Marshal Augereau's army corps and the enemy on Golymin, in front of Garnowo, resting his left on a wood that he had occupied by some battalions of infantry'; 'he rested his right on a small village in front of Golymin¹ by a great line of cavalry, which was supported by several lines of infantry'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'; 'the enemy was occupying it; he was driven out of it, as well as out of a small wood that he was holding with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon; so the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock'; 'Sire, we all generally thought that the enemy had 50,000 men'; 'all the troops that had evacuated Plonsk, Nasielsk, Nowemiasto and Ciechanow had united on Golymin'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The brigade arrived before Golymin on 26 December about 10 in the morning, and found, about a quarter of a league from that village and on this side of it, the cuirassiers of the Russian Guard and dragoons, the whole forming about 1,000 horses'; '« The Russians had 8 or 10 pieces in battery, the whole placed on a plain, and on their left a wood'; 'the Russian army, which came from Pultusk, was filing along the road that crosses Golymin to go to Makow; the roads were frightful, mainly for the French army, which had only cross-roads...'; 'the brigade Lasalle had the extreme left and was to charge the Russian artillery'; 'a thing as astonishing as it is inconceivable, there was not a horseman or a foot soldier in front of this brigade'; 'there were, it is true, 7 or 8 cannon which, had they been charged quickly, would perhaps not have fired;'; the report on Durosnel's brigade, 'the light cavalry brigade commanded by General Durosnel arrived before Pomorze about 10 o'clock; a strong Russian column of cavalry and infantry was filing past there'; 'the enemy formed much cavalry in line but did not answer with a single carbine shot'; 'his column went on filing past for a couple of hours'; 'according to the peasants, 20,000 men have passed here since last night, part heading for Pultusk and the other taking a road to the left half a league from here'; 'Pomorze, 26 December 1806, 2 in the afternoon'; 'the brigade general,'; 'Durosnel'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Watkowo, 26 December 1806, 10 in the evening'; 'Sire, General Durosnel is at Watkowo with his brigade. This village is three quarters of a league from Golymin and a quarter of a league from Kalenczyn, where the enemy is in very great numbers¹'; 'there are guns with this enemy force; they fired three shots from them, but one cannot judge whether they have several pieces'; 'the night prevents judging the enemy's strength'; 'the ground is so bad that one can go only at a very slow walk; those are the two causes that prevent my sending Your Majesty a more precise report; but as for his strength, it is considerable, to judge by the movement seen for two hours by the light of the fire of the village of Kalenczyn, which is burning'; 'two dragoons of the 4th regiment (division Klein) got through to here; they were wounded charging near Kalenczyn; they crossed the enemy force, which they say is very numerous, and all the cavalry; General Amey says the same'; the editor, 'at the beginning of the engagement the Russians were filing past, heading for Golymin and presenting their left flank'; 'this column came not from Pultusk but from Bielice; it was the one that had been seen on the 25th on the road from Nasielsk to Ciechanow by the dragoons' reconnaissance [printed 'réconnaissance']'; 'another Russian column, the one that had been repulsed at Sonsk on the 25th by the Grand Duke, was on the march from Ciechanow to Pultusk'; 'General Durosnel saw it file past from 10 o'clock to noon, at the height of Pomorze, heading for Golymin'; 'this column (division Panin) had about 12 kilometres to cover on a high road to reach the place of rendezvous fixed by General Buxhœvden for his army corps; it was this column that came out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon on the left flank of the 7th corps, while Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin'.

claims.value: The Grand Duke of Berg wrote to the Emperor from Makow at half past noon on 28 December that the enemy was retreating in disorder, apparently on the road to Rozan, and that the whole corps of Buxhœvden, which had fought at Golymin, had passed. General Corbineau wrote to the Emperor from Pultusk on 28 December that at Ostrolenka there must be a corps of 26,000 to 30,000 men under General Buxhœvden, which was fresh and had taken part neither in the combat of Pultusk nor in that of Golymin. In Höpfner, Field Marshal Kaminskoi had ordered on the 25th that General Count Buxhöwden set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place; General Dochtorow, commander of the 7th Division, sent his division off and stayed at Golymin in person with the Moscow Musketeer and Moscow Dragoon Regiments, or by Gallizin's report with the whole division; General Tschaplitz, who with General Pahlen joined Gallizin at 3 in the afternoon, had the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division; and Makow was Buxhöwden's headquarters, where the head of the retreating Russians arrived at midnight and joined the rear guard of the 5th Division, Tutschkow's. The editor has the division Panin making for the rendezvous General Buxhœvden had fixed for his army corps.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 487, 515, 517 and 518; Höpfner pp. 102, 122, 123 and 126). The Grand Duke's statement that Buxhœvden's whole corps had fought at Golymin is kept as a dispute and not resolved: Corbineau's letter of the same day denies it, and in Höpfner, of Buxhöwden's troops, only those of the 7th Division stood at Golymin, while the rear guard of his 5th Division was at Makow (our reading). The Grand Duke's letter was the one targeted follow-up for this entry; its sentence on Buxhœvden's corps continues on the next page, which was not read. Which of these troops Bodart's 22,000 counts is not shown. The forces at hand followed the field marshal's orders (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor'; 'Makow, 28 December 1806, half past noon'; 'the enemy is retreating in disorder; according to all the information I have obtained, he seems to have taken the road to Rozan'; 'the whole corps of Buxhœvden, which had fought at Golymin, has passed,' (p. 518, continued on p. 519, not read); Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'at Ostrolenka there must be a corps of 26,000 to 30,000 men commanded by General Buxhœvden, with General Kamenski the son and General Essen under his orders; this corps is fresh and took part neither in the combat of Pultusk nor in that of Golymin'; Höpfner, 'Field Marshal Kaminskoi, on his return to Pultusk, had announced the decision to accept battle at Pultusk, and on the 25th had ordered that for this General Count Buxhöwden should set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place;'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; '1) We follow here General Danielewski's statement, whereas according to Prince Gallizin's report General Dochtorow seems to have stayed behind with the whole division'; 'at Ciechanowo he united with General Tschaplitz, who, as mentioned, had had to advance from Golymin to Ciechanowo with the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'at Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk had indeed arrived on the morning of 27 December, but it changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at midnight the head reached Makow, 2¼ Meilen away, and joined the rear guard of the 5th Division, Tutschkow'; the editor, 'another Russian column, the one that had been repulsed at Sonsk on the 25th by the Grand Duke, was on the march from Ciechanow to Pultusk'; 'this column (division Panin) had about 12 kilometres to cover on a high road to reach the place of rendezvous fixed by General Buxhœvden for his army corps; it was this column that came out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon on the left flank of the 7th corps, while Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin'.

claims.value: Side A (French). In Höpfner, Marshal Augereau had to set the division Desjardins in motion on Golymin at 7½ in the morning and was to have the division Heudelet follow at 9; the Grand Duke of Berg was to march with the available cavalry reserve, it seems by Slubowo, and the light cavalry and 2 divisions of Davout's corps by Strzegocin, so that the French advanced on Golymin from three sides. The Grand Duke's advance guard was two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle; he came up at the head of a dragoon division, and the light cavalry brigade Marulaz came from Strzegocin; Augereau could bring up his troops on the bad roads only little by little, apparently without artillery yet; then came the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps, and Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières with the cavalry under General Rapp toward Zawady. The Grand Duke reported that he moved on Golymin with the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud and the division Klein, and that the heavy cavalry division arrived at nightfall and could take no part. Davout reported that General Morand moved on Golymin with the dragoons commanded by General Rapp, that he at once had the division Friant, in reserve, march, and that the 2nd division could arrive only at nightfall, as did 4 pieces of artillery of the 1st division; he had sent General Daultanne the order before noon to join him with the 3rd division, and the order was repeated. By the editor's note General Friant received the order to set out only when General Morand had recognised the Russian column on the march, so that his division could debouch from Garnowo only at 5 in the evening. In the 3rd corps's journal General Marulaz's chasseurs formed the 1st division's advance guard and joined the Grand Duke's advance guard under General Lasalle, who was followed by a brigade of dragoons with the Grand Duke at its head; the 2nd battalion of the 13th light and the 17th and 30th of the line formed in column, the 2nd brigade under General d'Honnières followed, and the two battalions of the 51st carried out the turning of the wood, with the 61st following in column; the division Morand stayed under arms throughout, and the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and ready to attack. General Rapp wrote that he was wounded at the head of the 5th and 9th dragoon regiments. In the editor's account the 2 divisions of the 7th corps set off at 9 in the morning, and the corps had neither artillery nor cavalry; its light cavalry had been sent toward Pomorze and Gostkowo, as the major general's letter of 6 in the morning told Augereau to order General Durosnel to go there with his light cavalry. General Curély recalled that the Grand Duke's troops had little infantry, thrown into the wood on their right; the editor's note says that the infantry in this wood was the 3rd corps's, the division Morand. The summary return Foucart prints of the troops that took part in the operations of the campaign of December 1806 gives the 7th corps 13,400 infantry and 1,050 cavalry, the 1st reserve cavalry corps 10,500 cavalry and the 3rd corps 21,500 infantry and 750 cavalry present under arms.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 122-125; Foucart t. I pp. 458, 459, 473-480, 482, 484, 485, 487, 488 and 490, and t. II the unnumbered page on leaf n486). No passage read gives side A's engaged strength. The return's 7th corps, 13,400 and 1,050, makes 14,450, its 3rd corps 22,250, and with the reserve cavalry's 10,500 the three rows make 47,200 (our arithmetic); the rows are whole corps in the middle of December, by Foucart's comment. At Golymin the 3rd corps had its 1st division and, from nightfall, its 2nd, while its 3rd division fought at Pultusk (the Pultusk entry, B377d), and which formations the reserve cavalry row covers is not shown. The 1st division is Morand's and the 2nd Friant's (our reading of Davout's letter, the editor's note on it and the journal). The account of the 7th corps is printed in the editor's smaller type and follows, by his introduction, General Desjardins's report and the 'Journal de marche du 3e corps d'armée', as printed. Curély's 'Murat' is the Grand Duke of Berg. Bodart's 27,000 is compared in claim bodart-strength. The forces at hand followed the Emperor's orders and the marshals' decisions (claims side-a-objectives and side-a-decisions), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'on the same day on which Marshal Lannes was in action against General Bennigsen's main forces at Pultusk, Marshal Augereau, on the strength of an order of Napoleon's from the headquarters at Lopaczyn, had had to set the division Desjardins in motion at 7½ in the morning from Golaczyzna near Sonsk on the Sonna on Golymin, into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there, and was to have the division Heudelet follow at 9 o'clock unless orders changing this arrived'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg was to march with the available cavalry reserve, as it seems, via Slubowo to Golymin, and the light cavalry and 2 divisions of Davout's corps to the same place via Strzegocin, so that the French thus advanced against Golymin from three sides'; 'it was the advance guard of the Grand Duke of Berg, two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle, which had pressed Colonel Kreuz and thrown him back on Garnowo, when the 3 squadrons of cuirassiers hurried up in support and, after some fighting to and fro, threw the enemy back to the wood'; 'at this time the Grand Duke of Berg also debouched on Garnowo at the head of a dragoon division and took in his advance guard, and at about the same time the light cavalry brigade Marulaz came up from Strzegocin'; 'Marshal Augereau, who on the bad roads could bring up his troops only little by little, but, as it seems, no artillery yet, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins, while he held back the second brigade at the village when he had become aware of his opponent'; 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'Sire, in accordance with Your Majesty's orders, I moved to Golymin with the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud and the division Klein;'; 'the heavy cavalry division arrived at nightfall and could take no part in the action; almost all the artillery had stayed in the bad roads'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Morand moved on Golymin with the dragoons commanded by General Rapp'; 'informed that this column had been seen by General Morand, I at once had the division Friant march, which was in reserve for either the 3rd or the 1st division'; 'the 2nd division could arrive only at nightfall¹, as could 4 pieces of artillery of the 1st division'; 'before noon I sent General Daultanne the order to come and join us with the 3rd division. This order was repeated'; the editor, '1. For fear that the enemy corps seen toward Bielice would debouch near Strzegocin to reach Pultusk behind the 3rd division, the marshal had put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours. It was only when General Morand had' (p. 475); 'recognised the Russian column on the march that General Friant received the order to set out; so his division could debouch from Garnowo only at 5 in the evening' (p. 476); the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'General Marulaz with his chasseurs, forming the advance guard of the 1st division, had taken 26 cannon, 80 caissons and 200 baggage vehicles that the Russians had abandoned in their retreat'; 'it was there that General Marulaz made his junction with the advance guard of the Grand Duke's cavalry, commanded by General Lasalle, who advanced with his hussar brigade on Garnowo, which the Cossacks had just set on fire' (p. 476); 'as they fled' (p. 477); 'he was followed by a brigade of dragoons at whose head was the Grand Duke'; 'while this cavalry was forming and moving forward, while the enemy cavalry was withdrawing on Golymin and the Russian infantry was preparing to defend the woods in front of that village, the 2nd battalion of the 13th light and the 17th and 30th of the line were forming in column by battalions'; 'the 2nd brigade, under the orders of General d'Honnières, was following'; 'the marshal, seeing that the enemy was withdrawing to the right, ordered General d'Honnières to turn the wood and advance on the road from Golymin to Pultusk'; 'this movement was perfectly carried out by the two battalions of the 51st, led by Colonel Baille'; 'the first of these battalions advanced as far as the wood of Osiek, while the 61st followed in column'; 'the division Morand stayed under arms throughout'; 'the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and was in a position to attack'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'I received my wound at the head of the 5th and 9th dragoon regiments at the moment when I intended to charge the Russian infantry and cavalry that were retreating before Marshal Davout's right'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'on the 26th at 9 in the morning the 2 divisions of the 7th corps, united at Galoczyn, set off in the direction of Golymin'; 'the 7th corps had neither artillery nor cavalry'; 'the light cavalry of the 7th corps had been directed from Lepki on the road from Ciechanow to Pultusk toward Pomorze and Gostkowo, to cut the communication and seize the enemy's baggage'; he must be there as early as possible'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The brigade Lasalle waited 3 hours for the troops of the Grand Duke of Berg, and they arrived slowly; there was little infantry'; '« Murat had thrown his little infantry into the wood that was on the right of his army corps (the same that was on the left of the Russians¹)'; It is the infantry of the 3rd corps, the division Morand, that was occupying this wood'; the return, 'summary return of the troops that took part in the operations of the campaign of December 1806'; 'present under arms'; 'infantry | cavalry'; '7th corps | 13,400 | 1,050'; '1st reserve cavalry corps | ″ | 10,500'; '3rd corps | 21,500 | 750'; 'the summary return above, which is correct since it rests on authentic documents, proves that in the middle of December the whole cavalry of the army did not reach 25,000 horses and that the infantry did not exceed 110,000 men present under arms,'.

claims.value: Bodart names Marshal Davoust as side A's commander and Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin as side B's. In Höpfner, Prince Gallizin posted the Russian troops before Golymin, where General Dochtorow, commander of the 7th Division, had stayed behind to take him in, and where Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz joined him at 3 in the afternoon; Marshal Augereau's corps, the Grand Duke of Berg with the cavalry reserve and 2 divisions of Marshal Davout's corps advanced on Golymin from three sides. The major general's orders of 26 December from Lopaczyn went separately to Marshal Augereau, the Grand Duke of Berg and Marshal Davout.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 122-124 and 126; Foucart pp. 458, 459 and 461). The commands were set before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. Bodart's Davoust is Davout, and his Gallitzin Höpfner's Gallizin. Whether any one commander directed side A is disputed (claim side-a-command); the marshals' and the Grand Duke's decisions on the field are in claim side-a-decisions, and side B's in claim side-b-command. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Gen.-Lt.' is General-Leutnant and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations; Höpfner, 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the same day on which Marshal Lannes was in action against General Bennigsen's main forces at Pultusk, Marshal Augereau, on the strength of an order of Napoleon's from the headquarters at Lopaczyn, had had to set the division Desjardins in motion at 7½ in the morning from Golaczyzna near Sonsk on the Sonna on Golymin, into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there, and was to have the division Heudelet follow at 9 o'clock unless orders changing this arrived'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg was to march with the available cavalry reserve, as it seems, via Slubowo to Golymin, and the light cavalry and 2 divisions of Davout's corps to the same place via Strzegocin, so that the French thus advanced against Golymin from three sides'; the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Augereau'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 6 in the morning'; 'the major general to the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 6 in the morning'; 'the major general to Marshal Davout'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, half past 7 in the morning'.

claims.value: Whether anyone directed side A as a whole. The editor writes that the combat of Golymin was fought against columns in retreat coming from different directions, by army corps that joined in a common action, but without any general direction during the whole of the engagement. A line in Foucart's small type after the 3rd corps's journal says that Marshal Davout received no order from the Grand Duke during the whole affair, and the journal has Marshal Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy an hour after nightfall nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps, the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack making any concert impossible. The major general's letter of 9 in the morning told the Grand Duke of Berg that, having arrived at Golymin, he would push Marshal Augereau's corps beyond Golymin if possible, while Marshal Davout's would stay at Golymin with one of its divisions on the high road to Pultusk. The Grand Duke reported that he linked up entirely with Augereau, separating himself from Davout, who held the wood throughout without being troubled by the enemy, and that he would have Davout told to be under arms at 6 the next morning and move on Golymin. The editor writes that the 7th corps bore the whole effort of the day, and that the reserve cavalry served as the link between the 3rd and 7th corps and above all prevented the enemy from enveloping Marshal Augereau.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 461, 462, 473, 476, 478, 480, 481, 483 and 487). A different account of side A's command from Bodart's, who names Marshal Davoust (claim bodart-commanders), kept as a dispute and not resolved. The 9 o'clock letter gave the Grand Duke the direction of Augereau's corps beyond Golymin (our reading); no passage read shows Davout commanding Augereau's corps or the Grand Duke's cavalry, or the Grand Duke giving Davout an order during the fight, and no report of Augereau's was seen. The editor's 'no general direction' is his judgement, and we read the small-type lines after the journal extract as his. English renderings (ours): the editor, 'the combat of Golymin was fought, as we shall see, in similar circumstances, against columns in retreat coming from different directions, by army corps that joined in a common action, but without there having been any general direction during the whole of the engagement'; the line, 'Marshal Davout received no order from the Grand Duke during the whole affair'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'an hour after nightfall Marshal Augereau's corps was at grips with the enemy nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps'; 'the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack made any concert impossible'; the major general, 'the major general to the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 9 in the morning'; 'the Emperor wishes you not to mistake the enemy's direction: having arrived at' (p. 461); 'Golymin, you will send detachments toward Pultusk to put yourself in communication with Marshal Lannes, who has the division Beker with him;' (p. 462); 'you will push, if possible, Marshal Augereau's corps forward beyond Golymin;'; 'that of Marshal Davout will remain at Golymin so that one of his divisions is on the high road to Pultusk to act if necessary, for we do not yet know whether Marshal Lannes has taken Pultusk'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'then I followed the enemy's movement with all my cavalry; I linked up entirely with Marshal Augereau, separating myself from Marshal Davout, who constantly held the wood without being troubled by the enemy, who then rested his left on Golymin'; 'tomorrow at 6 in the morning all my cavalry will be under arms and united with Marshal Augereau's corps at Golymin, to receive battle if the enemy prepares to attack us and to pursue him if he is retreating'; 'I shall have Marshal Davout told to be under arms at the same hour and to move on Golymin, to act there according to circumstances'; the editor, 'it was therefore the 7th corps that had to bear the whole effort of the day'; 'the reserve cavalry served as a link between the 3rd and 7th corps and above all prevented the enemy from enveloping Marshal Augereau'.

claims.value: Side A's decisions on the field, each attributed to the commander the passages name. Marshal Davout, learning that General Morand had seen the column reported at Bielice, at once had the division Friant march; by the editor's note he had put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours, for fear that the enemy corps seen toward Bielice would debouch near Strzegocin to reach Pultusk behind the 3rd division, until Morand had recognised the Russian column on the march; and he sent General Daultanne the order before noon to join him with the 3rd division, and the order was repeated. General Morand had the wood attacked and carried it, and about half past 3 directed the columns of the 1st brigade against the woods of Golymin; seeing the enemy withdrawing to the right, the marshal ordered General d'Honnières to turn the wood and advance on the road from Golymin to Pultusk (the 3rd corps's journal), and in Höpfner Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières with the cavalry under General Rapp toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat. Marshal Augereau, in Höpfner, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins and held back the second at the village when he became aware of his opponent, and the division Heudelet was to be pushed to the left on Watkowo on arriving, to lead the attack on Golymin from there; in the editor's account of the 7th corps the marshal, arriving as General Desjardins continued his division's march on Golymin, had its 2nd brigade (printed 'général Lefrauc', Lefranc later on the page) halt in the plain so as not to be outflanked, changed the direction of General Sarrut's brigade to between Watkowo and Golymin, ordered General Lefranc to carry the three pieces hampering the French movements, and ordered General Heudelet to make with his second brigade for the fire of Kalenczyn. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that he ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, that when the enemy moved by his right he followed with all his cavalry and linked up entirely with Augereau, separating himself from Davout, and that he then had Golymin reconnoitred.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 473-477, 480-482 and 487-489; Höpfner pp. 124 and 125). These were decisions taken on the field by side A's commanders: Davout, whom Bodart names, and Augereau and the Grand Duke of Berg, each commanding his own corps, with their generals; so the claim is tagged commander_created. It attributes each decision to the commander the passages name and none to a single commander for the whole (claim side-a-command). The journal's 'M. le Maréchal' is Davout, whom Höpfner names as sending the brigade d'Honnières forward, and the 'maréchal' of the editor's account of the 7th corps is Augereau, whom Höpfner names for holding back the second brigade (our reading). The 1st division is Morand's and the 2nd Friant's (our reading; claim side-a-strength). English renderings (ours): Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'yesterday¹, as I had the honour to report to you, a column of artillery, cavalry and infantry that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice'; 'informed that this column had been seen by General Morand, I at once had the division Friant march, which was in reserve for either the 3rd or the 1st division'; 'General Morand had the wood attacked that was' (p. 474); 'on the right of the plain occupied by Prince Joachim's cavalry, and carried it' (p. 475); 'before noon I sent General Daultanne the order to come and join us with the 3rd division. This order was repeated'; the editor, '1. For fear that the enemy corps seen toward Bielice would debouch near Strzegocin to reach Pultusk behind the 3rd division, the marshal had put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours. It was only when General Morand had' (p. 475); 'recognised the Russian column on the march that General Friant received the order to set out; so his division could debouch from Garnowo only at 5 in the evening' (p. 476); the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'about half past 3, the 1st brigade being formed, General Morand directed its columns to attack the woods of Golymin'; 'the marshal, seeing that the enemy was withdrawing to the right, ordered General d'Honnières to turn the wood and advance on the road from Golymin to Pultusk'; Höpfner, 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'Marshal Augereau, who on the bad roads could bring up his troops only little by little, but, as it seems, no artillery yet, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins, while he held back the second brigade at the village when he had become aware of his opponent'; 'the division Heudelet was to be pushed to the left on Watkowo on arriving, so as to make the attack on Golymin from there'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'having arrived at the village of Buskowo, General Desjardins, commanding the 1st division, seeing many troops on his left and having no cavalry, sent staff officers to reconnoitre: it was the enemy'; 'he closed up his division and continued his march on Golymin; but the marshal, arriving meanwhile, had the 2nd brigade (General Lefrauc [so printed]) halt in the plain so as not to be outflanked¹'; 'General Heudelet was forming the 2nd brigade, General Sarrut, as it arrived, so as to have it support the 1st division; but the marshal had its direction changed, ordering it to move between Watkowo and Golymin'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'during his march between Watkowo and Golymin, General Heudelet received the marshal's order to make with his second brigade for the fire of the burnt village of Kalenczyn'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'I then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and as he was setting about carrying out this order, the enemy faced about and the brigade Lasalle and that of General Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown'; 'then the enemy made a general movement by his right and sought to outflank Marshal Augereau's left'; 'then I followed the enemy's movement with all my cavalry; I linked up entirely with Marshal Augereau, separating myself from Marshal Davout, who constantly held the wood without being troubled by the enemy, who then rested his left on Golymin'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'.

claims.value: Side B's commanders' decisions, in Höpfner. Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, kept with him on the 25th the detachment cut off from General Sacken, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession; only toward evening did Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach him; the retreat was begun at nightfall, covered by detachments toward Pultusk and the Sonna, and he sent ahead to General Dochtorow to ask to be taken in with the 7th Division, as he was threatened from two sides. Dochtorow received the news at the moment when the field marshal's order to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk arrived; he had his division march off and stayed behind at Golymin in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in the prince. At Golymin, his troops being too exhausted to march on, Gallizin sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment to hold up the enemy when Colonel Kreuz reported the enemy cavalry approaching, and, though he soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of his troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow. He detached General Prince Tscherbatow to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn, posted the rest before Golymin with a reserve east of it astride the road to Makow, reinforced the Kostroma regiment, and sent forward two more battalions when the head of the division Morand threatened Tscherbatow's left flank; after they were thrown back he took them in and repulsed the following French in all further attacks by artillery fire. The troops kept in reserve, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively when Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières and General Rapp's cavalry toward Zawady. General Count Pahlen held the crossing at Lopaczyn on the 25th until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was blocked, retreated up the Sonna toward Ciechanowo, took up a position before the crossing at Sonsk to give the train time to file through, and united with General Tschaplitz at Ciechanowo; on the morning of the 26th both continued the retreat on Golymin, probably turning off to the left by Paluki after running into Durosnel's light cavalry brigade at Pomorze, and joined Gallizin on the Russian right wing at 3 in the afternoon. Toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, and Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, the artillery first, then the cavalry, the infantry and last the outposts.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102 and 122-126). Gallizin is side B's commander in Bodart (Gallitzin); these were his and his fellow generals' decisions within Bennigsen's and Kaminskoi's orders, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner names Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's work and the French reports as his sources for the combat and calls his account only an attempt (claim hoepfner-side-b); he follows Danielewski against Gallizin's report for Dochtorow's force, and his 'wohl' marks the cause of Pahlen's detour as his inference. In his account Durosnel's and Wathier's light cavalry brigades, without artillery, attacked Pahlen at Sonsk several times without doing the Russians any particular harm. English renderings (ours): 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'at that time the detachment cut off from General Sacken, which had stood below Lopaczyn, namely the Dnieper Musketeer and Little-Russian Cuirassier Regiments, arrived at Slubowo on its march to Strzegocin'; 'the prince kept it with him, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession'; 'only toward evening did General Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach [printed 'ereichte'] the prince, and free him from a very painful situation'; 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'Prince Gallizin sent ahead to Golymin to inform General Dochtorow of his approach, and to ask him to take him in with the 7th Division, as he [was] from two sides by the enemy' (p. 101); 'threatened' (p. 102); 'General Dochtorow had received this news at the moment when the field marshal's order had arrived' (p. 122); 'to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk' (p. 123); 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); 'while, to cover the left wing, thus probably in the direction of Strzegocin, 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons were pushed forward' (p. 124); 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'when the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment came under the fire of the enemy's skirmishers, it at once gave way, but Prince Tscherbatow led it forward again with the colour in his hand, and Prince Gallizin reinforced the regiment further with 1 battalion of the Taurian Grenadier Regiment'; 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as soon as Prince Gallizin had taken in the broken battalions, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'he finally saw himself compelled to begin the retreat up the Sonna in the direction of Ciechanowo'; 'when on the march he wanted to cross the river at Sonsk, he took up a position on the left bank in front of the crossing, to give the train time to file through'; 'in this position the light cavalry brigades Durosnel and Wathier came against him, but as they had not been able to bring artillery with them, they did not succeed, despite several attacks, in doing the Russians any particular harm,'; 'at Ciechanowo he united with General Tschaplitz, who, as mentioned, had had to advance from Golymin to Ciechanowo with the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division'; 'on the morning of 26 December both generals continued the retreat on Golymin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the march they had run into the light cavalry brigade Durosnel of Augereau's corps at Pomorze, and had probably been caused by this to turn off to the left on Paluki, so as to reach Golymin from there via Obiedzyn'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'first the artillery set off, then the cavalry followed, then the infantry, and last the outposts'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 123 (transcribed from the page image)

Division.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 124 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als das Kostromasche Musketier-Regiment in das Feuer der feindlichen Tirailleurs gerieth, wich es augenblicklich zurück, doch führte es der Fürst Tscherbatow mit der Fahne in der Hand wieder vor, und der Fürst Gallizin verstärkte das Regiment noch durch 1 Bataillon des Taurischen Grenadier-Regiments.

Bataillon des Taurischen Grenadier- und 1 Bataillon des Dneprowskischen Musketier-Regiments zur Besetzung der vorliegenden Gebüsche vor, unterstützt durch die noch nicht im Gefecht gewesenen 2 Schwadronen Pskowscher Dragoner.

citations.quote: Beide Bataillone vertheidigten die Gehölze mit großer Tapferkeit gegen mehrfache Angriffe der französischen Infanterie, ja sie gingen nach Ablegung des Gepäcks selbst zum Angriff über, wobei sie jedoch durch große Uebermacht überwältigt und auf Golymin zurückgeworfen wurden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 125 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Sobald der Fürst Gallizin die geworfenen Bataillone aufgenommen hatte, wies er die nachfolgenden Franzosen durch das Artillerie-Feuer mit Verlust in allen weitern Angriffen zurück.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 125 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der M. Davout sandte nunmehr die Brigade d'Honnières nebst der Kavallerie unter General Rapp in der Richtung auf Zawady vor, um so den Rückzug der Russen zu bedrohen; doch nun griffen auch die in der Reserve verbliebenen Truppen, und namentlich die des Generals Dochtorow, entscheidend ein.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 102 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Gr. Pahlen hatte am 25. mit seiner Arriergarde den Uebergang bei Lopaczyn so lange besetzt behalten, bis er sich überzeugt hatte, daß ihm die Straße nach Pultusk bereits verlegt und 2 Schwadronen Husaren abgeschnitten worden waren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 102 (transcribed from the page image)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 102 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In dieser Aufstellung traten ihm die leichten Kavallerie-Brigaden Durosnel und Wathier entgegen, doch da sie keine Artillerie hatten mit sich führen können, gelang es ihnen trotz mehrfacher Angriffe nicht, den Russen besonderen Abbruch zu thun,

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 102 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bei Ciechanowo vereinigte er sich mit dem General Tschaplitz, der, wie erwähnt, mit dem Pawlogrodschen Husaren-Regiment und einer reitenden Batterie der 7. Division von Golymin auf Ciechanowo hatte vorgehen müssen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 102 (transcribed from the page image)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 126 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Nachmittags 3 Uhr hatten sich auf dem rechten Flügel der Russen noch die Generale Pahlen und Tschaplitz von Ciechanowo her mit dem Fürsten Gallizin vereinigt.

claims.value: Bodart codes the engagement at Golymin on 26 December 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshal Davoust over the Russians under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin. The Grand Duke of Berg reported on 27 December that there had been several charges of cavalry and infantry, the French pushing the enemy and being pushed back in turn, but that in the end they forced him to yield the field of battle; that the enemy had vigorously disputed the ground and the affair lasted until 8 o'clock; that, when he then had Golymin reconnoitred, the enemy was driven out of it and out of a small wood, so that the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock; that the enemy seemed, by the few fires, to be retreating on Makow; and that Marshal Augereau's whole corps occupied Golymin, and Marshal Davout's whole corps, in front of Garnowo, the wood it had taken. In the 3rd corps's journal, when night had fallen, General Morand's troops took position at the edge of the woods within musket range of the road from Golymin to Pultusk, which was thus cut off from the enemy; the division Morand stayed under arms throughout, and the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and in a position to attack. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Lapisse pushed 2 companies into Golymin and, told that nobody was there, two battalions of the 16th light to cover the position; the 3rd battalion surprised and attacked a strong enemy column in retreat and took 160 men; the 16th then withdrew and took position behind Golymin, where it bivouacked; the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, the round shot, grapeshot and bullets falling on the French until 10 in the evening; and the marshal's headquarters was set up at the burnt village of Kalenczyn. The editor adds that the brigade Lapisse's reconnaissance of Golymin took place after 8 in the evening, as the Grand Duke says in his report, the Russians no longer passing through the village but going round it to reach the road to Makow, and, in a note citing the Grand Duke's report, that the combat ended only after 10 in the evening. General Corbineau learned at three quarters past 10 in the evening, from a returning patrol, that the enemy had withdrawn and that the French, Marshal Augereau's corps with part of the Grand Duke of Berg's cavalry, were masters of Kalenczyn. In Höpfner, toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest, and the head of the retreat reached Makow at midnight.
claims.rationale: Bodart's heading and entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Foucart and Höpfner from the page images (Foucart pp. 476, 478, 480, 482, 483, 487, 489, 491 and 493; Höpfner p. 126). The sources read agree that side B retreated on Makow in the night and that side A held Golymin; Höpfner holds that the combat went on without a decision until dark (claim hoepfner-result). Corbineau's note bears only the hour; the editor dates it to the 26th, later than his letter of 10 in the evening. The 'maréchal' of the editor's account is Augereau (our reading; claim side-a-decisions). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'there were then several charges of cavalry and infantry; we pushed the enemy; he pushed us back in his turn; but in the end we forced him to yield the field of battle to us'; 'the enemy vigorously disputed the ground; both sides fought with the greatest fury; the affair lasted until 8 o'clock'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'; 'the enemy was occupying it; he was driven out of it, as well as out of a small wood that he was holding with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon; so the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock'; 'it seems to me that the enemy is retreating on Makow, to judge by the few fires we see, though we have noticed that a large column had none, which' (p. 482); 'further confirms his retreat' (p. 483); 'Sire, here is our position: the whole of Marshal Augereau's corps occupying Golymin; the division Klein and the brigade Milhaud, Buskowo; Nansouty, Garnowo; Lasalle covering Marshal Augereau's infantry'; 'the whole of Marshal Davout's corps in front of Garnowo, occupying the wood it had taken this morning;'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'when night had fallen, to avoid skirmishes, always uselessly murderous, General Morand's troops took position at the edge of the woods, within musket range of the road from Golymin to Pultusk, which was thus cut off from the enemy'; 'the division Morand stayed under arms throughout'; 'the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and was in a position to attack'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'General Lapisse, 1st brigade of the 1st division, pushes 2 companies into Golymin; told that nobody is there, they want to occupy the village; then two battalions of the 16th light infantry are pushed forward to cover this position'; 'a strong enemy column that was making its retreat is surprised and attacked by the 3rd battalion of this regiment; the enemy fired a discharge of grapeshot at 40 paces; the liveliest musketry begins; this battalion takes 160 men'; 'the 16th withdraws and takes position behind Golymin, where they bivouac'; 'the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, after having, however, lost many men; in short, the round shot, the grapeshot, the bullets and the hail did not stop falling on us until 10 in the evening'; 'the marshal's headquarters was set up in the burnt village of Kalenczyn, between Buskowo and Golymin'; 'the reconnaissance of the village of Golymin by the brigade Lapisse took place after 8 in the evening, as the Grand Duke says in his report'; 'the Russians were no longer passing through the village, but going round it to rejoin the road to Makow'; '1. The combat ended only after 10 in the evening. (Report of the Grand Duke of Berg.)'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to His Majesty the Emperor, at Paluki'; 'three quarters past 10'; 'I learn this moment from a returning patrol that the enemy, who was between Kalenczyn and here, has withdrawn and that the French are masters of Kalenczyn; it is Marshal Augereau's corps that is there, with part of the cavalry of His Highness Prince Murat'; the editor, 'this undated note is of the 26th at three quarters past 10 in the evening, and later than the preceding one'; Höpfner, 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at midnight the head reached Makow, 2¼ Meilen away, and joined the rear guard of the 5th Division, Tutschkow'.

claims.value: Höpfner gives a different result in his account of the combat at Golymin on 26 December. On the Russian right wing the first brigade of Augereau's corps went forward to the attack, and when the French continued the attack they came into the Russians' musket and canister fire and were repulsed; the advance of the second brigade seems to have had no better success, and the French advance over the broken ground before Golymin was soon checked, so that the combat gradually ran out into a skirmishing fight back and forth across the meadows until dark. Where the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps came up, the two Russian battalions sent into the woods were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin, but Gallizin, having taken them in, repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire. When Davout then sent the brigade d'Honnières with General Rapp's cavalry toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat, the Russian reserves, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively; the cavalry fight that followed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the French pursued the Russian cavalry they came under the fire of the infantry and artillery and had to return with great loss, Rapp being severely wounded; so the combat went on there too without a decision, despite the unequal forces, until dark. Toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, and Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest; the news of the battle won at Pultusk, which reached General Buxhöwden's headquarters at Makow on the morning of 27 December, changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier. Höpfner calls his account only an attempt to make the course of the combat to some extent clear, the Russian and French reports differing so completely.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 122 and 124-126). A different result from Bodart's frozen victory of the French (claim bodart-winner), kept as a dispute and not resolved: Höpfner names no winner, but has neither wing decided before dark and the Russians continuing a retreat already decided (our reading). His account rests on reports he calls completely different from one another (claim hoepfner-side-b). English renderings (ours): 'combat at Golymin on 26 December.¹)'; 'meanwhile the first brigade of Augereau's corps had gone forward to the attack'; 'when the French continued the attack, they came into the musket and canister fire of the Russians, to the latter of which they had nothing to oppose, and were repulsed'; 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); 'so the combat on the Russians' right wing gradually ran out into a skirmishing fight, back and forth across the meadows, until dark'; 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as soon as Prince Gallizin had taken in the broken battalions, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'the cavalry went to meet General Rapp'; 'the cavalry fight that then developed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment particularly distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the Russian cavalry was nevertheless' (p. 125); 'once forced to go back behind its infantry, the French in pursuing came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery in such a way that they had to return with great loss and General Rapp was severely wounded' (p. 126); 'so here too the combat went on without a decision, despite the unequal forces, until dark'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk had indeed arrived on the morning of 27 December, but it changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier'; 'the Russian report of Prince Gallizin in Plotho's Tagebuch, the report in General Danielewski's work and the French reports in Mathieu Dumas etc. on this combat differ so completely from one another that the account given here may be regarded only as an attempt to make the course of the combat to some extent clear'.
