claims.value: Bodart gives the French losses as about 1,000 men (4 generals, 53 officers), and the Russian losses as 600 men (19 officers) killed and wounded and 200 prisoners, together 800 men; he lists French Brigade-General Fénérols with a dagger.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed losses, read from the page image in the frame transcription; his officer-loss table for the engagement is not in the frame transcription. His Russian 600 with 19 officers fit the killed and wounded of Gallizin's report in Höpfner, 3 officers and 80 men dead and 16 officers and 473 men wounded, 572 with 19 officers (claim side-b-losses-reported; our arithmetic), rounded up by his rule (claim bodart-strength; our comparison), and his 200 prisoners are close to the report's 203 missing, though below it despite that rule (our comparison); with the missing the report makes 775 (our arithmetic), against Bodart's 800. His French about 1,000 matches no figure in the passages read: the loss line Foucart prints after the 3rd corps's journal gives its 1st division 9 killed and 8 officers and 205 men wounded, 222 (our arithmetic), and the editor's account of the 7th corps gives its 1st division 34 killed and 326 wounded and its 2nd division 9 killed and 53 wounded, 422 (our arithmetic), together 644 for the three divisions without the cavalry (our arithmetic); the French, by Höpfner, estimated their loss as equal to that of the Russians (claim side-a-losses-reported). The generals the passages name as killed or wounded are Fénérolz killed and Rapp and Lefranc wounded (our count); whom Bodart's 4 generals count is not shown. Bodart's Fénérols is the Grand Duke's Fénérolz. The explanatory pages transcribed (pp. 45-48) do not define the dagger; the Grand Duke's report says that Fénérolz was killed by a cannon shot. Which source Bodart used was not checked. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'French losses: about 1,000 men (4 generals, 53 officers) | Russian losses: 600 men (19 officers) killed and wounded, 200 [men] prisoners, together 800 men'; '† French Brigade-General Fénérols'; 'Frz.' is französisch (listed as 'fz., frz., franz.'), 'Russ.' russisch (listed as 'russ.'), 'Gen.' Général en chef oder General, 'Offz.' Offizier, 'verw.' verwundet and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations, which lists 'gfg., gef.' as gefangen; 'Verl.', 'Gefg.', 'zus.', 'ca.' and 'u.' are not in it as printed, and we read them as Verlust, Gefangene, zusammen, circa and und, and '„' as the ditto mark for 'M.'; 'fz.' is französisch and 'Brig.-Gen.' Brigade-General in Bodart's list of abbreviations; the explanatory pages transcribed (pp. 45-48) do not define the dagger.

claims.value: Side A's losses as reported. Marshal Davout wrote on 26 December that General Rapp had been put out of action by fire, his arm broken, that the light cavalry of the 3rd corps with the reserve cavalry had suffered much, and that General Morand had had men wounded by musketry and a horse killed. A loss line in Foucart's small type after the 3rd corps's journal gives the 1st division 9 men killed and 8 officers and 205 men wounded. General Rapp wrote on 27 December that a ball had broken his left arm above the elbow: as he advanced at a very slow walk on a mass of cavalry, it opened, and some platoons of infantry it had masked fired a volley that wounded only him. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that they suffered much from the enemy's artillery, that General Fénérolz was killed by a cannon shot, and that Marshal Augereau and Generals Lasalle and Milhaud had several horses killed under them. General Curély recalled that General Lasalle led the reunited brigade under the enemy cannon, where it stayed until midnight, its general having two horses killed under him and men and horses falling at every moment. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Lefranc's brigade, ordered to carry three pieces, was covered with grapeshot at 50 paces and stopped by a marsh; its column fell back hastily some 200 paces, and with General Lefranc wounded Colonel Habert took command of the brigade; on the 26th the 1st division had 34 killed and 326 wounded and the 2nd division 9 killed and 53 wounded. In Höpfner the French estimate their loss as equal to that of the Russians, but he thinks it probable that, in the disadvantageous situation in which they had to fight, they lost considerably more; in the cavalry fight the French, pursuing the Russian cavalry, came under the fire of the Russian infantry and artillery and had to return with great loss, General Rapp being severely wounded.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 473, 475, 476, 478-482, 484 and 486-489; Höpfner pp. 125 and 126). No total for side A is given in the passages read. The loss lines make 222 for the 3rd corps's 1st division and 422 for the 7th corps's two divisions (our arithmetic), without the reserve cavalry, the light cavalry and the 3rd corps's 2nd division; whether the 1st division's line counts General Rapp's dragoons is not shown, and the line names no source. Bodart's about 1,000 is compared in claim bodart-losses. Höpfner's view that the French lost more is his inference from their situation. English renderings (ours): Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Rapp moved to our right and, with his brilliant courage, although the ground was very marshy, wanted to cross swords; the enemy cavalry fell back; the Russian infantry did the same, but after firing; General Rapp was put out of action by the fire; his arm is broken'; 'the light cavalry of the 3rd corps, which was with the reserve cavalry, suffered much'; 'General Morand had men wounded by musketry and had a horse killed'; the line, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; '1st division. — Killed: men, 9. Wounded: officers, 8; men, 205'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'Sire, Marshal Davout will no doubt have reported to Your Majesty on the affair that took place yesterday' (p. 478); 'in front of Garnowo. There I received a ball that broke my left arm above the elbow...' (p. 479); 'I was advancing on this mass of cavalry in the hope of making it cross swords, still at a very slow walk, being unable to go faster; all of a sudden it opened to right and left, and some platoons of infantry that it masked fired a volley at us that wounded only me'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'the enemy in his turn was totally overthrown and driven back to his lines of infantry; it was then that we suffered much from the enemy's artillery'; 'Sire, I owe the greatest praise to the dragoon division; it was that which restored the affair four or five times; we have to regret General Fénérolz, who was killed by a cannon shot'; 'Marshal Augereau and Generals Lasalle and Milhaud had several horses killed under them'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The brigade having been reunited, General Lasalle led it under the enemy cannon. It stayed there until midnight without moving'; 'to give an idea of the loss this brigade suffered from the enemy cannon, in punishment for its retrograde movement: the general, who was at its head, had two horses killed under him; men and horses fell at every moment: nobody moved; not even a murmur was heard....'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'; 'the column fell back hastily some 200 paces; it was rallied, formed in square, and stayed in position in front of the burnt village, between Buskowo and Goly-' (p. 488); 'min. General Lefranc having been wounded in this attack, Colonel Habert took command of the brigade' (p. 489); 'on the 26th the 1st division had 34 killed and 326 wounded; the 2nd division [printed 'là 2e'], 9 killed and 53 wounded'; Höpfner, 'the French estimate their loss as equal to that of the Russians, but it is probable that, in the disadvantageous situation in which they had to fight, they lost considerably more than the Russians'; 'the cavalry fight that then developed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment particularly distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the Russian cavalry was nevertheless' (p. 125); 'once forced to go back behind its infantry, the French in pursuing came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery in such a way that they had to return with great loss and General Rapp was severely wounded' (p. 126).

claims.value: Side B's losses as reported. In Höpfner Prince Gallizin gives the Russian loss as 3 officers and 80 men dead, 16 officers and 473 men wounded and 203 men missing; in Höpfner's account of his retreat from Lopaczyn on the 25th, General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons. Marshal Davout reported on 26 December that the 1st division, on its march on Golymin, forced the enemy to abandon 13 pieces of ordnance. The 3rd corps's journal says that General Marulaz's chasseurs, the 1st division's advance guard, had taken 26 cannon, 80 caissons and 200 baggage vehicles that the Russians had abandoned in their retreat, as he came out of the village of Ostarzewo, and that the enemy, after a lively resistance, threw down his packs to charge with the bayonet but was forced to abandon the wood and the field of battle, leaving on it a great number of dead and 4,000 packs. General Rapp wrote on 27 December that the artillery the enemy had abandoned and the French had gathered up would be very difficult to get out of the places where it was. General Curély recalled that the cavalry of the right took from the enemy a good number of men and horses and two standards. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the 3rd battalion of the 16th light took 160 men, one piece of cannon and one caisson remained in French hands, the enemy lost many men before continuing his retreat, and the 1st division took 10 pieces of cannon in the affair. The report on General Durosnel's brigade, signed by him at Pomorze at 2 in the afternoon, says that the brigade took stragglers, ammunition caissons, carts loaded with flour and some baggage there at noon, and that two squadrons of the 7th chasseurs, sent after the enemy toward Gotskowo, had taken 4 pieces of cannon and several caissons on the road.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101, 102 and 126; Foucart pp. 473, 476-480, 484-487 and 489-491). Gallizin's figures make 83 dead and 489 wounded, 572 killed and wounded with 19 officers, and 775 with the missing (our arithmetic); Bodart's figures are compared in claim bodart-losses. The gun counts are not added: Davout's 13 pieces, Marulaz's 26 cannon, the 10 pieces of the 7th corps's 1st division and the one piece left in French hands, and the 4 pieces on the Gotskowo road may count the same guns more than once, and several were abandoned on the roads rather than taken in the fight (our reading). The 160 men are the only prisoners counted in the passages read; Curély's men and horses and the stragglers taken at Pomorze are not counted. Pahlen's gun was left before the engagement, and the guns and vehicles taken on the French march and on the Gotskowo road are reported with their place and time. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the Russians' loss is given by Prince Gallizin as 3 officers and 80 men dead, 16 officers and 473 men wounded, and 203 men missing'; 'General Count Pahlen had stayed behind at Lopaczyn with a rear guard — the 21st Jäger Regiment, the Sumy Hussar Regiment and a horse battery'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'on its march on Golymin the 1st division forced the enemy to abandon 13 pieces of ordnance'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'General Marulaz with his chasseurs, forming the advance guard of the 1st division, had taken 26 cannon, 80 caissons and 200 baggage vehicles that the Russians had abandoned in their retreat'; 'he was coming out of the village of Ostarzewo'; 'the enemy put up a lively resistance'; 'he ended by throwing down his packs to charge with the bayonet, but the fire and boldness of the skirmishers and the battalions forced him to abandon the wood and the field of battle, on which he left a great number of dead and 4,000 packs'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'Marshal Davout must also have reported to Your Majesty on the artillery that the enemy abandoned and that we have picked up; it will be very difficult to get it out of the places' (p. 479); 'where it is' (p. 480); Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The cavalry of our right was not stopped in its charge, and it overthrew the enemy, who was also charging on his side. Our cav-' (p. 485); 'alry took from the enemy a good number of men and horses and two standards' (p. 486); the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'General Lapisse, 1st brigade of the 1st division, pushes 2 companies into Golymin; told that nobody is there, they want to occupy the village; then two battalions of the 16th light infantry are pushed forward to cover this position'; 'a strong enemy column that was making its retreat is surprised and attacked by the 3rd battalion of this regiment; the enemy fired a discharge of grapeshot at 40 paces; the liveliest musketry begins; this battalion takes 160 men'; 'one piece of cannon and one caisson remained in our hands'; 'the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, after having, however, lost many men; in short, the round shot, the grapeshot, the bullets and the hail did not stop falling on us until 10 in the evening'; 'the 1st division took 10 pieces of cannon in this affair'; Durosnel, 'the light cavalry brigade commanded by General Durosnel arrived before Pomorze about 10 o'clock; a strong Russian column of cavalry and infantry was filing past there'; 'the brigade entered Pomorze at noon; it took stragglers there, ammunition caissons, carts loaded with flour and some baggage'; 'two squadrons of the 7th chasseur regiment were detached after the enemy as far as Gotskowo, in accordance with His Majesty's orders [printed 'ordes']. On the road they took 4 pieces of cannon and several' (p. 490); 'caissons. The report of their arrival at Gotskowo has not yet come in' (p. 491); 'Pomorze, 26 December 1806, 2 in the afternoon'; 'the brigade general,'; 'Durosnel'.

claims.value: Golymin is a market town in Russian Poland, 20 km north-west of Pultusk (Bodart). In Höpfner the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin made the approach very difficult; the broken ground before Golymin, whose approach the Russian artillery commanded, soon set limits to the French advance, and the fight on the Russian right ran out into skirmishing back and forth across the meadows; Prince Tscherbatow was detached to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn, and two Russian battalions defended the woods; on the Russian night march guns and wagons had sunk in the mud above the axles. Marshal Davout wrote that the ground on the right where General Rapp sought to cross swords was very marshy and that the roads were frightful. General Rapp wrote that the bad weather had made the ground absolutely impracticable, the horses sinking to the breast, that cavalry had never been seen to move over such frightful ground, and that all the country from Nasielsk to Garnowo was nothing but a great marsh. The Grand Duke of Berg found the enemy on Golymin in front of Garnowo, with his left on a wood held by some battalions of infantry and his right on a small village in front of Golymin, Kalenczyn by the editor's note; his postscript says the roads were frightful and the country full of marshes. General Curély recalled the Russians placed on a plain with a wood on their left, filing along the road through Golymin to Makow, the roads being frightful, above all for the French, who had only cross-roads. The editor calls Golymin the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position. In the editor's account of the 7th corps an impracticable marsh stopped General Lefranc's brigade, and General Heudelet found himself entirely in the plain. The report on General Durosnel's brigade found the ground at Pomorze too muddy for any bold stroke, and his postscript the roads dreadful, the horses in mud up to the belly; General Corbineau found the ground so bad that one could go only at a very slow walk.
claims.rationale: Bodart's location line, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101 and 122-125; Foucart pp. 473, 475, 478-480, 483, 484, 487, 488 and 490-492). The ground and the weather were given, so the claim is tagged inherited; the Russian position was Gallizin's choice (claim side-b-command). Höpfner's Kalęczyn is Foucart's Kalenczyn (our reading). Höpfner's plan of the area of Golymin, to which his note refers, was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '1806 26/12. Engagement at Golymin (6.)'; 'victory of the French (27,000 men) under Marshal Davoust over the Russians (22,000 men) under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin'; '(market town in Russian Poland, 20 km north-west of Pultusk)'; Höpfner, 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); 'so the combat on the Russians' right wing gradually ran out into a skirmishing fight, back and forth across the meadows, until dark'; 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); 'while, to cover the left wing, thus probably in the direction of Strzegocin, 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons were pushed forward' (p. 124); 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'guns and wagons sank in the mud above the axles, and the very bad weather also made the march extraordinarily difficult'; '1) See the plan of the area of Golymin'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Rapp moved to our right and, with his brilliant courage, although the ground was very marshy, wanted to cross swords; the enemy cavalry fell back; the Russian infantry did the same, but after firing; General Rapp was put out of action by the fire; his arm is broken'; 'the roads are frightful; it will take all night to bring up the pieces of the other divisions'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'the bad weather had made the ground absolutely impracticable; the horses sank to the breast; it was impossible for us to go faster than at a very slow walk'; 'cavalry has never been seen to move in such frightful ground'; 'all the country I have crossed from Nasielsk to Garnowo is nothing but a great marsh'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'my advance guard made its junction with Marshal Davout's corps at the village of Garnowo at the same time as I was reconnoitring by my left Marshal Augereau's army corps and the enemy on Golymin, in front of Garnowo, resting his left on a wood that he had occupied by some battalions of infantry'; 'he rested his right on a small village in front of Golymin¹ by a great line of cavalry, which was supported by several lines of infantry'; 'P.S. I have come back here to feed the' (p. 483); 'horses of the cavalry. The roads are frightful and the country full of marshes' (p. 484); the editor, '1. Village of Kalenczyn'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The Russians had 8 or 10 pieces in battery, the whole placed on a plain, and on their left a wood'; 'the Russian army, which came from Pultusk, was filing along the road that crosses Golymin to go to Makow; the roads were frightful, mainly for the French army, which had only cross-roads...'; the editor, 'one understands from this that the combat was fierce at Golymin, the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position in this affair'; 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'; 'General Heudelet, judging rightly that, being entirely in the plain and having a long line of cavalry before him, he would soon be charged, at once ordered the formation of a single square'; Durosnel, 'the light cavalry brigade commanded by General Durosnel arrived before Pomorze about 10 o'clock; a strong Russian column of cavalry and infantry was filing past there'; 'the ground was too muddy to allow any bold stroke'; 'Pomorze, 26 December 1806, 2 in the afternoon'; 'the brigade general,'; 'Durosnel'; 'the roads are appalling; the horses have mud up to the belly'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Watkowo, 26 December 1806, 10 in the evening'; 'the ground is so bad that one can go only at a very slow walk; those are the two causes that prevent my sending Your Majesty a more precise report; but as for his strength, it is considerable, to judge by the movement seen for two hours by the light of the fire of the village of Kalenczyn, which is burning'.

claims.value: Side A's means. In Höpfner Marshal Augereau could bring up his troops on the bad roads only little by little, apparently without artillery yet, and the first brigade of his corps, attacking, had nothing to oppose to the Russian canister. Marshal Davout reported that the 2nd division and 4 pieces of artillery of the 1st division could arrive only at nightfall, that the roads were frightful and it would take all night to bring up the guns of the other divisions, and that the night was being used to bring up the artillery and replace the cartridges, of which the 1st division was short at the end of the day; the 3rd corps's journal says that the 1st division had fought without artillery, which had not been able to follow because of the bad roads. General Rapp wrote that they had met the French artillery stuck in the mud everywhere, and that he had just learned that the bread wagons had had to be unloaded at Nasielsk because they could not continue. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that the heavy cavalry division arrived at nightfall and could take no part, that almost all the artillery had stayed on the bad roads, and that he had come back to Garnowo to feed the cavalry's horses. General Curély recalled that the brigade Lasalle waited 3 hours for the Grand Duke's troops, who arrived slowly, and that a single cannon, which managed to reach the line, fired toward the enemy without reaching him. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the corps had neither artillery nor cavalry; the editor also writes that the reserve cavalry's other troops certainly did not set off before half past 10 and came into line only about one in the afternoon.

claims.value: Side B's means, in Höpfner. On the night march from Slubowo the troops, and still more the horses, were completely exhausted, and were allowed some rest already ¾ Meilen from Slubowo; guns and wagons sank in the mud above the axles, and the very bad weather made the march extraordinarily difficult. Prince Gallizin's column reached Golymin at 8 in the morning of the 26th after a march of 13 hours, his troops so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; he decided to stay halted as long as their state urgently required, and sent ahead to Makow to prepare everything for their reception and refreshment. He took the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars back into reserve because they were very exhausted. The two battalions in the woods laid down their packs before going over to the attack. General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons. In the retreat the artillery set off first.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102 and 123-126); he names no source for the state of the troops beyond the reports he follows for the combat (claim hoepfner-side-b). The exhaustion was inherited from the retreat, while the halt at Golymin was Gallizin's decision (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. The guns, caissons and baggage the Russians abandoned on the roads are in claim side-b-losses-reported. English renderings (ours): 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'already ¾ Meilen from Slubowo the troops were allowed some rest; they, and still more the horses, were completely exhausted'; 'guns and wagons sank in the mud above the axles, and the very bad weather also made the march extraordinarily difficult'; 'at 8 in the morning of the 26th the column, after a march of 13 hours, reached Golymin, 1½ Meilen away'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons'; 'first the artillery set off, then the cavalry followed, then the infantry, and last the outposts'.

claims.value: Side A's information. At 6 in the morning the major general wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg that the Emperor, not knowing what was happening at Strzegocin and Golymin, wished to wait for news, above all from Marshal Davout, and that a letter just received from Davout said he had not been able to reach Strzegocin the day before because of frightful roads and would attack the enemy's camp there that morning if it had not been evacuated in the night; at half past 7 he wrote to Davout that the enemy in front of him would surely have retreated on Golymin, and that he must march with caution and keep his corps well together, as there were many scattered and cut-off columns; at 9 he wrote to the Grand Duke that the enemy had left Strzegocin at 2 in the morning for Golymin, that he should not mistake the enemy's direction, and that it was not yet known whether Marshal Lannes had taken Pultusk. Davout reported that a column that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice the day before, that he had sent Colonel Exelmans there, who left with 200 horses (the editor's note), and that on his arrival he found the enemy before him. By the editor's note a squadron of dragoons had seen an enemy corps in bivouac with much artillery beyond Smolechowo on the 25th; Captain Scitivaux of the 8th dragoons reported from Smolechowo on 26 December that he was placed there with a squadron by Davout's orders to observe the march of the enemy, who was retreating on Pultusk, Golymin and Sturze (?); and, by the 3rd corps's journal as the note reports it, the marshal sent out parties all night to learn the march of two enemy columns, one seen on the 25th toward Bielice and the other withdrawn a quarter of a league beyond Strzegocin. By another note Davout put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours, for fear that the corps seen toward Bielice would debouch behind his 3rd division, until General Morand had recognised the Russian column on the march. The editor thinks the Grand Duke, told at half past 6 in the morning that Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin, probably sent part of his light cavalry that way for news. The Grand Duke reported that he reconnoitred Augereau's corps and the enemy by his left and later had Golymin reconnoitred, judged by the few fires that the enemy was retreating on Makow, had with the others generally thought the enemy 50,000 men, had no news of Marshal Lannes and no word from Watier's or Durosnel's cavalry, and excused his report as perhaps a little disjointed, being extremely tired. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Desjardins, seeing many troops on his left and having no cavalry, sent staff officers to reconnoitre: it was the enemy; General Heudelet, surrounded by Cossacks and hussars, forbade firing until the enemy was on the bayonets, the darkness being so great, the position such and the French cavalry so close that firing would have been imprudent; a battalion of the 14th, in reserve to support the 16th light, could not fire for fear of killing French soldiers; the 7th light was separated from the 7th corps from the beginning of the engagement, and at 10 in the evening General Amey, at Watkowo with Generals Corbineau and Durosnel, did not know where his division general was. In the 3rd corps's journal the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack made any concert with Augereau's corps impossible. General Corbineau wrote at 10 in the evening that, doubting whether a very great movement of cavalry around the burning village of Kalenczyn was the enemy's, General Durosnel had it reconnoitred and attacked, and was assured it was Russian because a corporal of the attacking picket was wounded by a lance; that the night prevented judging the enemy's strength; that General Durosnel had joined General Amey, of the division Heudelet, who had the 7th light infantry regiment with him and did not know where his division general was; and that the enemy's movement was very undetermined, now toward his right, apparently from Kalenczyn to Makow, now toward his left and the road from Kalenczyn to Golymin.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 459-462, 473-476, 478, 480, 482, 483 and 487-493). The headquarters letters show the Emperor without news at 6, presuming the enemy's direction at half past 7 and knowing it by 9 (our reading). The Grand Duke's 50,000 is his and his officers' general opinion (claim foucart-side-b). The 'marshal' of the 3rd corps's journal is Davout (our reading; claim side-a-decisions). The information available followed partly from the ground and the dark and partly from the commanders' own reconnaissance, so the phase is unresolved. the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'having arrived at the village of Buskowo, General Desjardins, commanding the 1st division, seeing many troops on his left and having no cavalry, sent staff officers to reconnoitre: it was the enemy'; 'during his march between Watkowo and Golymin, General Heudelet received the marshal's order to make with his second brigade for the fire of the burnt village of Kalenczyn'; 'he felt the need to keep his square formation, and had reason to congratulate himself on it, for at that very moment he was surrounded by Cossacks and hussars'; 'the darkness was so great and the position such that it would have been imprudent to fire'; 'our cavalry was close by, and the least mistake could have become extremely disastrous'; 'the general therefore forbade firing until the enemy was on the bayonets'; 'a battalion of the 14th, which was in reserve to support the 16th light, cannot fire for fear of killing our own men'; 'the 7th light, directed on Watkowo, was separated from the 7th corps from the beginning of the engagement'; 'at 10 in the evening Generals Corbineau and Durosnel were at Watkowo with General Amey, who did not know where his division general was'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'an hour after nightfall Marshal Augereau's corps was at grips with the enemy nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps'; 'the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack made any concert impossible'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Watkowo, 26 December 1806, 10 in the evening'; 'having noticed a very great movement of cavalry around the village of Kalenczyn, which is on fire, we were in doubt whether it was the enemy's; General Durosnel had it reconnoitred and attacked. He' (p. 491); 'was assured that this cavalry was Russian because a corporal of the picket charged with the attack had been wounded by a lance thrust' (p. 492); 'the night prevents judging the enemy's strength'; 'General Durosnel has made his junction here with General Amey, of the division Heudelet. This general has the 7th light infantry regiment with him. He does not know where his division general is'; 'the enemy's movement is very undetermined: at times he is seen heading toward his right, and would then seem to want to go from Kalenczyn to Makow; at times, on the contrary, he is seen taking a direction to his left, and would then take the road that goes from Kalenczyn to Golymin'.

claims.value: Side B's information, in Höpfner. Prince Gallizin waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession on the 25th, and marched with enemy parties accompanying him on both sides; on the march to Golymin he had General Dochtorow informed that the French were advancing from all sides. At Golymin Colonel Kreuz reported the enemy cavalry approaching and threatening to attack, the prince soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, and soon enemy infantry, the head of the division Desjardins, also appeared beyond Ruskowo at the edge of the wood. General Count Pahlen held the crossing at Lopaczyn on the 25th until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off; on the 26th he and General Tschaplitz ran into Durosnel's light cavalry brigade at Pomorze and were probably caused by this to turn off to the left by Paluki. The news of the battle won at Pultusk reached General Buxhöwden's headquarters at Makow on the morning of 27 December.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102, 122, 123 and 126). He names Gallizin's report, Danielewski and the French reports as his sources for the combat (claim hoepfner-side-b), and his 'wohl' marks the cause of Pahlen's detour as his inference. The information followed from the retreat and from the generals' own observation, so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'the prince kept it with him, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession'; 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'soon, however, enemy infantry also appeared beyond Ruskowo at the edge of the wood, the head of the division Desjardins of Augereau's corps'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'on the morning of 26 December both generals continued the retreat on Golymin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the march they had run into the light cavalry brigade Durosnel of Augereau's corps at Pomorze, and had probably been caused by this to turn off to the left on Paluki, so as to reach Golymin from there via Obiedzyn'; 'at Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk had indeed arrived on the morning of 27 December, but it changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier'.

claims.value: Side A's objectives, in the orders given by the Emperor on the morning of the 26th. The major general wrote to Marshal Augereau at 6 in the morning that the Emperor intended him to send off one division at half past 7 to march on Golymin, with the other ready to leave about 9, but, if he heard a very heavy cannonade toward Strzegocin, to direct his corps there without further order to support Marshal Davout; and to order General Durosnel to go with his light cavalry between Ciechanow and Golymin to Pomorze and Gostkowo, to cut the road and gather up all the enemy's baggage. He wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg at the same hour that his cavalry was to wait for orders, and to Davout at half past 7 that he would have followed the enemy to Golymin, for which Augereau was also making, to fall on the enemy's flanks if he stood, but that if the enemy had gone toward Pultusk he should follow him there. At 9 he wrote to the Grand Duke to set out with his cavalry and fall on the enemy's flanks, the roads being bad, so that the artillery and baggage must be his; having arrived at Golymin, he was to send detachments toward Pultusk to communicate with Marshal Lannes and to have Augereau's corps pushed beyond Golymin if possible, while Davout's corps stayed at Golymin with one of its divisions on the high road to Pultusk, to act if necessary, as it was not yet known whether Lannes had taken Pultusk. A dispatch at 9 told Augereau of the enemy's movement on Golymin and the Grand Duke's march, with the order to march some battalions briskly to support the cavalry. In Höpfner the French thus advanced on Golymin from three sides, Augereau's division Desjardins into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there. Davout reported that he had sent General Daultanne the order before noon to join him with the 3rd division, and that the order was repeated. The Grand Duke wrote that at 6 the next morning all his cavalry would be under arms with Augereau's corps at Golymin, to receive battle if the enemy prepared to attack and to pursue him if he was retreating.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 458, 459, 461, 462, 473, 475, 480 and 483; Höpfner p. 122). The objectives were set from above by the Emperor's orders through the major general and adapted on the field by the marshals and the Grand Duke (claim side-a-decisions), so the claim's single phase is unresolved. The 9 o'clock dispatch to Augereau is printed as a summary, not as the letter's text (our reading). The 3rd division of Davout's corps fought at Pultusk (the Pultusk entry, B377d). English renderings (ours): Foucart, 'orders given by the Emperor on the morning of the 26th'; the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Augereau'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 6 in the morning'; 'the Emperor's intention, Marshal, is that you send off one division at half past 7 to march on Golymin; your other division will be ready to leave about 9 in the morning'; 'if, however, you heard a very heavy cannonade toward Strzegocin, you would direct there, without' (p. 458); 'further order, your army corps to support Marshal Davout, who in that case would have a serious affair there' (p. 459); 'give General Durosnel the order to go with his light cavalry between Ciechanow and Golymin, to the point of Pomorze and Gostkowo, so as to cut the road and gather up all the enemy's baggage; he must be there as early as possible'; 'the major general to the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 6 in the morning'; 'the Emperor, not knowing what is happening at Strzegocin and Golymin, wishes to wait for news, above all from Marshal Davout; His Majesty's intention is that your cavalry wait for orders'; 'the major general to Marshal Davout'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, half past 7 in the morning'; 'the enemy who was in front of you will surely have retreated and withdrawn on Golymin; in that case you will have followed him there'; 'Marshal Augereau is also making for that point, to fall on the enemy's flanks if he stands up to you; but if the enemy had gone toward Pultusk, it is proper that you follow him there'; 'the major general to the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 9 in the morning'; 'the enemy arrived at Strzegocin yesterday evening; he left it at 2 in the morning for Golymin; the Emperor's intention is that you set out with your cavalry and fall on his flanks; General Beaumont is pursuing him from behind; the roads being bad, the artillery and the baggage must be yours'; 'the Emperor wishes you not to mistake the enemy's direction: having arrived at' (p. 461); 'Golymin, you will send detachments toward Pultusk to put yourself in communication with Marshal Lannes, who has the division Beker with him;' (p. 462); 'you will push, if possible, Marshal Augereau's corps forward beyond Golymin;'; 'that of Marshal Davout will remain at Golymin so that one of his divisions is on the high road to Pultusk to act if necessary, for we do not yet know whether Marshal Lannes has taken Pultusk'; 'dispatch to Marshal Augereau, at 9 in the morning, to warn him of the enemy's movement on Golymin and of the march of the Grand Duke of Berg; order to march some battalions briskly to support the cavalry'; Höpfner, 'on the same day on which Marshal Lannes was in action against General Bennigsen's main forces at Pultusk, Marshal Augereau, on the strength of an order of Napoleon's from the headquarters at Lopaczyn, had had to set the division Desjardins in motion at 7½ in the morning from Golaczyzna near Sonsk on the Sonna on Golymin, into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there, and was to have the division Heudelet follow at 9 o'clock unless orders changing this arrived'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg was to march with the available cavalry reserve, as it seems, via Slubowo to Golymin, and the light cavalry and 2 divisions of Davout's corps to the same place via Strzegocin, so that the French thus advanced against Golymin from three sides'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'before noon I sent General Daultanne the order to come and join us with the 3rd division. This order was repeated'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'tomorrow at 6 in the morning all my cavalry will be under arms and united with Marshal Augereau's corps at Golymin, to receive battle if the enemy prepares to attack us and to pursue him if he is retreating'.

claims.value: Side B's objectives. In Höpfner, General Bennigsen's order reached Prince Gallizin only toward evening on the 25th: to retreat on Golymin. Field Marshal Kaminskoi had announced the decision to accept battle at Pultusk and on the 25th ordered General Count Buxhöwden to set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place. Gallizin asked General Dochtorow to take him in with the 7th Division; Dochtorow, ordered by the field marshal to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk, sent his division off and stayed at Golymin in person to take in the prince. Gallizin decided to stay halted at Golymin as long as the state of the troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow; toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow and he followed about 9. At Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk, which arrived on the morning of 27 December, changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier. The editor writes that at the beginning of the engagement the Russians were filing toward Golymin, presenting their left flank; that another column, the division Panin, marching from Ciechanow on Pultusk, was making for the rendezvous General Buxhœvden had fixed for his army corps; and that on learning of General Panin's arrival the first Russian column made a general movement by its right to join him; Golymin was the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and Foucart, read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101, 102, 122, 123 and 126; Foucart p. 487). Höpfner gives the orders and decisions without naming a document beyond the reports he follows (claim hoepfner-side-b). The halt at Golymin and the retreat to Makow were Gallizin's decisions within his superiors' orders (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created. The editor's 'key of the position' is his judgement, and his division Panin is compared with Höpfner's Pahlen and Tschaplitz in claim foucart-side-b. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'only toward evening did General Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach [printed 'ereichte'] the prince, and free him from a very painful situation'; 'Field Marshal Kaminskoi, on his return to Pultusk, had announced the decision to accept battle at Pultusk, and on the 25th had ordered that for this General Count Buxhöwden should set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place;'; 'Prince Gallizin sent ahead to Golymin to inform General Dochtorow of his approach, and to ask him to take him in with the 7th Division, as he [was] from two sides by the enemy' (p. 101); 'threatened' (p. 102); 'General Dochtorow had received this news at the moment when the field marshal's order had arrived' (p. 122); 'to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk' (p. 123); 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk had indeed arrived on the morning of 27 December, but it changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier'; the editor, 'at the beginning of the engagement the Russians were filing past, heading for Golymin and presenting their left flank'; 'another Russian column, the one that had been repulsed at Sonsk on the 25th by the Grand Duke, was on the march from Ciechanow to Pultusk'; 'this column (division Panin) had about 12 kilometres to cover on a high road to reach the place of rendezvous fixed by General Buxhœvden for his army corps; it was this column that came out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon on the left flank of the 7th corps, while Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin'; 'as soon as it learned of General Panin's arrival, the 1st Russian column made a general movement by its right to join him'; 'one understands from this that the combat was fierce at Golymin, the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position in this affair'.

claims.value: Side A attacked. Bodart has a victory of the French. In Höpfner the Grand Duke of Berg's advance guard, two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle, had pressed Colonel Kreuz and thrown him back on Garnowo when the 3 squadrons of cuirassiers hastened up in support and, after some fluctuating fighting, threw the enemy back toward the wood; the French cavalry deployed opposite the Russian cavalry; the first brigade of Augereau's corps went forward to the attack, and when the French continued the attack they came into the Russians' musket and canister fire and were repulsed; the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success; the division Heudelet went forward to the attack from Watkowo; the head of the division Morand, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, and the French infantry attacked the woods repeatedly; and Marshal Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières with the cavalry under General Rapp toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat. Davout reported that General Morand had the wood attacked and carried it, and that the enemy infantry, coming forward to retake it, was repulsed after a very lively engagement; in the 3rd corps's journal Morand directed the columns of the 1st brigade to attack the woods of Golymin about half past 3, and General Rapp moved to the right with his dragoons. Rapp wrote that he was wounded as he intended to charge the Russian infantry and cavalry retreating before Davout's right, and that the enemy at once retreated without the French being able to reach him. The Grand Duke reported that the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud, formed in two lines, engaged the enemy while the advance guard of the division Morand drove the Russian infantry out of the wood; that he then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and that as Nansouty set about it the enemy faced about and the brigades Lasalle and Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown; that the brigade Milhaud, on the right, charged the enemy in flank while the head of the division Klein charged him in front; that Augereau, pushing a large enemy corps before him, himself directed his march on Golymin; and that the division Desjardins, manoeuvring by its right, occupied the small village in front of Golymin, which the enemy had burnt on abandoning it, while Augereau's 2nd division marched straight on the village of Golymin, pushing the enemy before it. General Curély recalled that Augereau drew up almost all his infantry in square and in mass in the middle of the plain, within cannon range of the road on which the Russians were filing; that the attack was ordered about 2 in the afternoon; that the brigade Lasalle, on the extreme left, was to charge the Russian artillery but had gone barely twenty paces when a cry of 'Halt! Halt!' was heard and repeated in both regiments, and that, though the enemy did not fire a cannon shot, the two regiments broke and retreated, with neither horseman nor foot soldier in front of the brigade; and that the cavalry of the right was not stopped in its charge and overthrew the enemy, who was charging too; the editor calls it the panic of the brigade Lasalle. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the marshal halted the 2nd brigade in the plain so as not to be outflanked, about 2 o'clock by the editor's note; General Amey's brigade took Watkowo; General Sarrut's brigade, sent between Watkowo and Golymin, was approaching the enemy when some Russian cavalry appeared on its flank while 3 pieces of cannon battered it in front; General Heudelet ordered a square, whose file fire dispersed a charge on its right; and General Lefranc's brigade, ordered to carry the three pieces, went to the attack and was covered with canister at 50 paces, and a terrible fusillade began on both sides, but an impracticable marsh prevented the infantry from going further; it was night. The 3rd corps's journal has Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy, nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps, an hour after nightfall. Side B halted and stood: in Höpfner Prince Gallizin's troops, on reaching Golymin at 8 in the morning, were too exhausted to march on; when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, reported the enemy cavalry approaching and threatening to attack him, the prince sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment to hold up the enemy and, though he soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow. The two battalions he sent forward defended the woods and went over to the attack themselves after laying down their packs; once Gallizin had taken them in, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire; the troops kept in reserve, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively; and the cavalry went to meet General Rapp: in the cavalry fight that followed, without decisive result, when the Russian cavalry was once forced back behind its infantry, the French pursuing it came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery and had to return with great loss.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A's corps attacked side B's detachment, which had halted before Golymin because its troops were too exhausted to march on; side B's cavalry charges and the battalions' attack in the woods were made in the fight for its position before Golymin and do not, by the brief, make the defender an attacker (our reading). The times are kept as printed: the attack ordered about 2 in the afternoon (Curély), the halt of Augereau's 2nd brigade about 2 (the editor's note), Morand's attack about half past 3 (the 3rd corps's journal) and Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy an hour after nightfall (the same journal). Where the passages name who ordered an attack, it was a marshal or general on the field (claim side-a-decisions), so the claim is tagged commander_created; whether anyone directed side A as a whole is disputed (claim side-a-command). Höpfner's 'der Fürst' and 'Er' on p. 123 are Prince Gallizin, named in the sentence on Dochtorow before them; the 'maréchal' of the editor's account of the 7th corps is Augereau; and the brigade that the Russian cavalry and the 3 pieces met is General Sarrut's, named in the sentence before (our reading). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'it was the advance guard of the Grand Duke of Berg, two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle, which had pressed Colonel Kreuz and thrown him back on Garnowo, when the 3 squadrons of cuirassiers hurried up in support and, after some fighting to and fro, threw the enemy back to the wood'; 'the French cavalry deployed opposite the Russian cavalry'; 'meanwhile the first brigade of Augereau's corps had gone forward to the attack'; 'when the French continued the attack, they came into the musket and canister fire of the Russians, to the latter of which they had nothing to oppose, and were repulsed'; 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as soon as Prince Gallizin had taken in the broken battalions, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'the cavalry went to meet General Rapp'; 'the cavalry fight that then developed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment particularly distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the Russian cavalry was nevertheless' (p. 125); 'once forced to go back behind its infantry, the French in pursuing came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery in such a way that they had to return with great loss and General Rapp was severely wounded' (p. 126); Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Morand had the wood attacked that was' (p. 474); 'on the right of the plain occupied by Prince Joachim's cavalry, and carried it' (p. 475); 'the enemy infantry moved forward to retake this wood'; 'after a very lively engagement it was repulsed'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'about half past 3, the 1st brigade being formed, General Morand directed its columns to attack the woods of Golymin'; 'General Rapp moved to the right with his dragoons....'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'I received my wound at the head of the 5th and 9th dragoon regiments at the moment when I intended to charge the Russian infantry and cavalry that were retreating before Marshal Davout's right'; 'the enemy at once made his retreat without our being able to reach him'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud formed on two lines and engaged the enemy in that order, while the advance guard of the division Morand succeeded' (p. 480); 'in driving the Russian infantry out of the wood' (p. 481); 'I then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and as he was setting about carrying out this order, the enemy faced about and the brigade Lasalle and that of General Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown'; 'the brigade Milhaud, which was on the right, charged the enemy in flank, while the head of the division Klein charged him in front'; 'all this was going on in front of Golymin, while Marshal Augereau, who was pushing a large enemy corps before him, was himself directing his march on Golymin'; 'the division Desjardins manoeuvred by its right and came to occupy the small village in front of Golymin, which the enemy had set on fire on abandoning it'; 'the 2nd division of Marshal Augereau's corps was marching straight on the village of Golymin, pushing before it' (p. 481); 'the enemy, who constantly outflanked it by its left, which it refused;' (p. 482); Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« On the left of Murat's corps Marshal Augereau arrived with almost all his infantry, which he drew up in square and in mass in the middle of the plain, within cannon range of the road on which the Russians were filing, who presented their left flank to us'; '« About 2 in the afternoon the attack was ordered; the right of the line of our cavalry had its right resting on the wood'; 'the brigade Lasalle had the extreme left and was to charge the Russian artillery'; 'scarcely had this brigade gone twenty paces forward to charge when a cry of « Halt! Halt! » was heard, and this cry was repeated in the two regiments'; '« The enemy did not fire a cannon shot, and yet the two regiments broke, went to the rear and rallied a half quarter of an hour away;'; 'a thing as astonishing as it is inconceivable, there was not a horseman or a foot soldier in front of this brigade'; '« The cavalry of our right was not stopped in its charge, and it overthrew the enemy, who was also charging on his side. Our cav-' (p. 485); 'alry took from the enemy a good number of men and horses and two standards' (p. 486); the editor, 'apart from the curiosity of this account, which lets us witness the panic of the brigade Lasalle on the field of bat-' (p. 486); 'tle, General Curély gives us valuable information on the different phases of the action' (p. 487); 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'he closed up his division and continued his march on Golymin; but the marshal, arriving meanwhile, had the 2nd brigade (General Lefrauc [so printed]) halt in the plain so as not to be outflanked¹'; '1. It might have been about 2 o'clock'; 'the 2nd division, General Heudelet, was hastening its march; as soon as the 1st brigade of that division, 7th light, General Amey, was formed, it made for Watkowo, which it took'; 'General Heudelet was forming the 2nd brigade, General Sarrut, as it arrived, so as to have it support the 1st division; but the marshal had its direction changed, ordering it to move between Watkowo and Golymin'; 'it was approaching the enemy when some Russian cavalry appeared on its flank, while 3 pieces of cannon battered it in front'; 'General Heudelet, judging rightly that, being entirely in the plain and having a long line of cavalry before him, he would soon be charged, at once ordered the formation of a single square'; 'scarcely had this manoeuvre been carried out when a charge came on its right, but it wavered at the sight of the square's good bearing, and the file fire directed at it dispersed it in an instant'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'; the journal, 'an hour after nightfall Marshal Augereau's corps was at grips with the enemy nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps'.

citations.quote: 1806 26./12. TREFFEN bei Golymin (6.)
Sieg der Franzosen (27.000 M.) unter Marschall Davoust über die Russen (22.000 M.) unter Gen.-Lt. Fürst Gallitzin.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 123 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Kaum hatte sich indessen das Detaschement gesammelt und einigermaßen geordnet, als der Oberst Kreuz, der mit den 2 Schwadronen Sumscher Husaren die Arriergarde gemacht hatte, die Meldung sandte: die feindliche Kavallerie rücke an und drohe ihn anzugreifen.

citations.quote: Der Fürst schickte alsbald 3 Schwadronen des Kürassier-Regiments St. Georg zur Verstärkung vor, um den Feind aufzuhalten, überzeugte sich aber bald, daß er mit sehr bedeutenden feindlichen Kräften zu thun bekommen werde.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 123 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Er entschloß sich dessenungeachtet, so lange halten zu bleiben, als es der Zustand der Truppen dringend erforderte und dann den Rückzug nach Makow fortzusetzen, wohin sogleich vorausgesandt wurde, um Alles zum Empfang und zur Erfrischung der Truppen vorzubereiten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 3 (1851), p. 123 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Es war die Avantgarde des Großherzogs von Berg, zwei Regimenter Husaren unter dem General Lasalle, welche den Obersten Kreuz bedrängt und auf Garnowo zurückgewiesen hatten, als die 3 Schwadronen Kürassiere zur Unterstützung herbeieilten und nach einigem wechselnden Gefecht den Feind nach dem Walde zurückwarfen.

citations.quote: näherung im hohen Grade erschwerten, und auch selbst, als die Division Heudelet eingetroffen war und von Watkowo zum Angriff vorging, wurde sie eine Zeitlang von entgegengeworfener russischer Kavallerie aufgehalten, und als diese sich zurückzog, sahen die Franzosen ihrem Vorgehen über das durchschnittene Terrain vor Golymin, dessen Zugang durch die russische Artillerie beherrscht wurde, bald Schranken gesetzt.

Bataillon des Taurischen Grenadier- und 1 Bataillon des Dneprowskischen Musketier-Regiments zur Besetzung der vorliegenden Gebüsche vor, unterstützt durch die noch nicht im Gefecht gewesenen 2 Schwadronen Pskowscher Dragoner.

claims.value: The passages read name no works on either side. In Höpfner Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn, pushed forward 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons to cover the left wing, and posted the rest before Golymin, with a reserve east of it astride the road to Makow; the dissolved ground and wet meadows before Golymin made the approach of the second brigade of the division Desjardins very difficult, and the access over the broken ground before Golymin was commanded by the Russian artillery. The Grand Duke of Berg reported the enemy resting his left on a wood he had occupied by some battalions of infantry and his right on a small village in front of Golymin, Kalenczyn by the editor's note, with a great line of cavalry supported by several lines of infantry; and that, when he had Golymin reconnoitred, the enemy was driven from it and from a small wood he held with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon. General Curély recalled 8 or 10 Russian pieces in battery, the whole placed in a plain, with a wood on their left. In the editor's account of the 7th corps an impracticable marsh prevented General Lefranc's brigade, ordered to carry the three pieces of cannon, from going further.
claims.rationale: Coded none_named: the cited passages describe side B's position and the ground the French crossed and name no entrenchments, redoubts, abatis or other works used in the fighting. Woods, bushes, a village, a battery, dissolved ground or a marsh are not works under the brief. none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed; Höpfner's plan of the area of Golymin (his p. 122, note 1) was not inspected. Prince Gallizin took up the position on the day (claim side-b-command) on ground neither side made, so the phase is unresolved. Höpfner's Kalęczyn is Foucart's Kalenczyn (our reading). English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); 'while, to cover the left wing, thus probably in the direction of Strzegocin, 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons were pushed forward' (p. 124); 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'my advance guard made its junction with Marshal Davout's corps at the village of Garnowo at the same time as I was reconnoitring by my left Marshal Augereau's army corps and the enemy on Golymin, in front of Garnowo, resting his left on a wood that he had occupied by some battalions of infantry'; 'he rested his right on a small village in front of Golymin¹ by a great line of cavalry, which was supported by several lines of infantry'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'; 'the enemy was occupying it; he was driven out of it, as well as out of a small wood that he was holding with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon; so the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock'; the editor, '1. Village of Kalenczyn'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The Russians had 8 or 10 pieces in battery, the whole placed on a plain, and on their left a wood'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'.
