open_questions: Deferred: Höpfner's plan of the area of Golymin (his p. 122, note 1), not inspected; his p. 100 (the start of the sentence that ends at the top of p. 101 on a force that should have withdrawn on Pultusk and had not arrived), seen only in the OCR, and p. 103 (the end of the sentence on the field marshal's conduct begun on p. 102) and p. 127 (the end of the sentence on the 5th Division's march of the 27th begun on p. 126), not read; his figures for Buxhöwden's army, to which the 7th Division belonged, not looked for; Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I, p. 494 (the note the editor prints after Corbineau's of three quarters past 10) and p. 519 (the rest of the Grand Duke's letter of 28 December), not read; General Lasalle's letter to the Grand Duke of 28 December, printed whole on p. 518, not used; Bodart's officer-loss table for the engagement, not in the frame transcription; General Desjardins's report and the 'Journal de marche du 3e corps d'armée' (so printed) that the editor follows for the 7th corps, the 3rd corps's journal beyond the extract, Prince Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's work and Mathieu Dumas, not seen. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: both sides' engaged strength. Bodart gives 27,000 French and 22,000 Russians without battalions, squadrons or guns; Höpfner gives no total for either side and names the Russian regiments only in part; the French documents give impressions (very numerous; an infantry ten times stronger; 50,000 by the Grand Duke's general opinion; 20,000 past Pomorze by peasants' hearsay, not a count of the force at Golymin), and the summary return gives whole corps in the middle of December, not the divisions and brigades engaged. The one targeted follow-up, the Grand Duke's letter of 28 December (p. 518), added his statement that the whole corps of Buxhœvden had fought at Golymin, against Corbineau's letter of the same day and Höpfner's troops of the 7th Division. Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's figures or a return of the 7th corps for late December could narrow the gap.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the result (a French victory, Bodart, with the field yielded to the French in the Grand Duke's report; no decision on either wing until dark, Höpfner); side A's command (Davoust, Bodart; no general direction during the whole of the engagement, the editor, with no order from the Grand Duke to Davout during the whole affair by a small-type line after the 3rd corps's journal and no concert possible after nightfall by the journal); whether Buxhœvden's corps fought at Golymin (the whole corps, the Grand Duke; neither at Pultusk nor at Golymin, Corbineau; troops of the 7th Division, Höpfner); Dochtorow's force (the Moscow Musketeer and Moscow Dragoon Regiments, Danielewski as Höpfner follows him; the whole division, Gallizin's report); side B's strength (22,000, Bodart; 50,000 by general opinion, the Grand Duke); side A's losses (about 1,000 with 4 generals and 53 officers, Bodart; the loss lines of three divisions; equal to the Russians' by the French estimate and probably considerably more, Höpfner); side B's losses (600 killed and wounded and 200 prisoners, Bodart; 3 officers and 80 men dead, 16 officers and 473 men wounded and 203 men missing, Gallizin's report in Höpfner); the guns taken (13 pieces, Davout; 26 cannon, the 3rd corps's journal; 10 pieces by the 7th corps's 1st division and one more with a caisson, the editor's account; 4 pieces on the road to Gotskowo, the report on Durosnel's brigade); the times given (the attack ordered about 2 in the afternoon, Curély; Augereau's 2nd brigade halted about 2, the editor's note; Morand's attack about half past 3 and Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy an hour after nightfall, the 3rd corps's journal); the general killed (Fénérols, Bodart; Fénérolz, the Grand Duke); who repulsed the Russians at Sonsk on the 25th (the Grand Duke, the editor; Durosnel's and Wathier's light cavalry brigades attacked Pahlen there, Höpfner; that the editor's column is Pahlen's is our comparison); and Curély's Russian army from Pultusk, which the editor corrects to a column from Bielice.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his Russian 600 with 19 officers fit the killed and wounded of Gallizin's report in Höpfner, rounded up, and his 200 prisoners are close to its 203 missing, while his 27,000, 22,000 and French about 1,000 match no figure in the passages read); Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I and t. II, one family with his Campagne de Prusse (the same author's edition of the French side's documents: the major general's orders of 26 December, Davout's letter, Captain Scitivaux's report, the extract of the 3rd corps's journal, Rapp's and the Grand Duke's letters of 27 December, Curély's recollections, the report on Durosnel's brigade, Corbineau's letter and note of 26 December and letter of 28 December, the Grand Duke's letter of 28 December, the editor's narrative and notes, his account of the 7th corps after Desjardins's report and the 3rd corps's journal of march, so printed, his small-type loss line and the summary return); Höpfner, Bd. 3 (the Prussian side's history of the campaign, the same work and family as his other volumes; he names Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's work and the French reports in Mathieu Dumas for this combat, says they differ so completely that his account is only an attempt, and follows Danielewski for Dochtorow's force).
